blocks.p: RISC-V is an open instruction set architecture (ISA): the instructions, registers and memory model that software sees, which anyone may implement without paying a royalty. This laboratory runs RV32I, the 32-bit base integer instruction set, with the M extension for multiplication and division.

Krste Asanović and the graduate students Yunsup Lee and Andrew Waterman started RISC-V in May 2010 in the Parallel Computing Laboratory (Par Lab) of the University of California, Berkeley, which David Patterson directed; the first manual (2011) is by Waterman, Lee, Patterson and Asanović. The RISC-V Foundation was founded in 2015 with 36 founding members, and in March 2020 the RISC-V International Association was incorporated in Switzerland. RISC-V International maintains and ratifies the specifications.

Why it matters: an open, royalty-free ISA lets companies, universities and individuals design processors for it and share cores and tools, instead of licensing an instruction set from one company. Its base is small and regular, with standard extensions added as needed, which makes it practical for teaching processor design, as in this laboratory.

Where it is used, for example: Espressif's ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C6 microcontrollers have RISC-V processors; Raspberry Pi's RP2350 has two Hazard3 RISC-V cores beside two Arm Cortex-M33 cores; Western Digital announced its open-source SweRV RISC-V core in 2018, with the goal of moving one billion of its processor cores to RISC-V; NVIDIA presented in 2016 its plan to replace its Falcon controller with its own RISC-V core.
The architecture is specified in RISC-V International's manuals. They have no DOI; the links are the publishers' own pages.

blocks.p: The MAVILERA RISC-V Laboratory runs RISC-V programs in your browser and shows how a processor executes them. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded.

ol: Type a program in the editor, or open one from Templates in the toolbar: short programs that each show one idea, with a note at the top on what to try.
Press Assemble (Ctrl+Enter). Errors are marked in the editor and explained in the console, with a hint.
Step through the program with Step (F10) and Step back (Shift+F10), or run it with Run (F5).
Watch the registers, memory and counters change. The last register written is marked ◆.
Switch to a processor view (Single-cycle, Multicycle, Pipelined) to see the same program on a datapath, one clock cycle at a time.

blocks.p: A program ends with the system call exit (li a7, 93 and ecall, with the exit code in a0) or with the pseudo-instruction halt, a jump to itself. The processor views stop at halt.

dl: The instruction-level simulator for RV32I and the M extension: editor, listing with machine words in hexadecimal and binary, instruction inspector, registers, call stack, counters, memory and console.

A processor that executes every instruction in one clock cycle. The paths the instruction uses are highlighted on the datapath; the Control tab shows the decoders, the Timing tab the critical paths and the clock period.
A processor that takes several shorter cycles per instruction, steered by a state machine. Show the datapath or the state diagram; Instruction ▶ runs all cycles of one instruction (F11).

A five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) with forwarding, load-use stalls, flushes and an optional branch predictor. The hazard unit can be set from none to complete to see what each part does. The pipeline diagram shows every instruction in every cycle.
In each processor view, the Waveforms tab draws chosen signals over the clock cycles run so far, as a timing diagram; select a cycle to go to it. The axis orders cycles; it is not hardware timing.
Runs the program of the editor to its halt on all three processors and tabulates instructions, cycles, CPI, clock period, execution time and speed-up, with illustrative delays.

blocks.p: The processor views implement a subset of RV32I (no byte or half-word loads and stores, no M extension) and have small memories. Use the ISA view for anything else.

ul: Assembly: the RV32I and M instructions, pseudo-instructions such as li, la, mv, j, call, ret, beqz and halt, and the directives .text .data .rodata .bss .word .half .byte .ascii .asciz .string .space .align .balign .equ .set.
System calls: a7 = 93 exits with the code in a0; a7 = 64 writes a2 bytes from the address in a1 to the console (a0 = 1).
C: choose C under Language. A teaching subset is compiled one statement at a time, in a plain or a register translation; point at a line on either side to see its counterpart.
GCC output: open a .s file made with gcc -S; it is adapted for the simulator and the changes are listed.
Point at an instruction in the editor for what it does; completion suggests mnemonics and registers.
Breakpoints: click a line number in the editor or an address in the listing (B on a row).
Watchpoints: tick a register's eye to stop when it is written; double-click a memory word, or use Watch, to stop when that word is written.
Step back undoes one step at a time, back to the start of the run (the oldest steps of a very long run are dropped, with a message).
Step over runs a call to its return; Step out runs to the return of the current procedure; Run to cursor stops at the editor's line.
The calling-convention check reports faults in the console, such as a procedure that returns with a register changed that it must keep.

The uninitialised-value check reports, in the console, a register read before anything wrote it, or a stack word loaded before anything stored it. It is the simulator's own check; saving ra or s0–s11 in a prologue is not reported.
A run that does not halt stops after a large number of instructions and says where it is looping.

dl: Step / step back (in a processor view, one clock cycle)
Step over / step out (in the multicycle view, one instruction)
Leave the editor (Tab inside it indents)
In the listing: move, show the fields, set a breakpoint
Resize panes (Shift for larger steps; Enter restores)
Open its details in a processor view

blocks.p: The Memory button chooses the memory model: ideal memory, main memory without a cache, or main memory with an instruction cache (L1I) and a data cache (L1D). For a cache you choose the size, block size, number of ways, replacement and write policy. The settings are illustrative designs for teaching, not those of any real processor. Any change restarts the program.

The Cache tab of the Memory and cache panel shows the last access of each cache, how the address finds its line, the lines as sets and ways (valid, dirty, tag, words), and the counters of hits and misses. In the instruction-level view the caches show their state at the current instruction (the run is replayed from the start); the button on the tab counts the whole run at once.

Under the last access the animation shows the access step by step. Replay plays it again, Next step goes one step at a time and Show all steps shows them together; with reduced motion switched on in the system, all the steps are shown at once.
The group Caches and memory in Templates opens short programs that each show one idea; each sets the memory model it needs.

The profile "ISA with traps and devices" (Profile list, instruction-level view) adds the laboratory's platform: a GPIO at 0x4000_0000 with eight LEDs, four switches and a push button, a machine timer at 0x4000_1000 and a UART at 0x4000_2000, with Zicsr instructions, traps and interrupts.

The Peripherals tab of the Memory and cache panel draws the board: LEDs glow with the GPIO output, the switches and the button are yours to operate with the mouse or the keyboard (Space or Enter), the timer's count fills against its compare value, and the interrupt lines to the processor light while a request is active. Below it are the processor's mode and trap registers, every device register (read without side effects), the UART terminal where you can type bytes for the receiver, a table of the interrupts requested with the cycles from request to handler, and the stimulus script of pin events. Each pin you change is added to the script at the current cycle, so Reset and Step back replay it.

dl: In this profile ecall is a trap: compiled C programs and the exit and write calls of the plain ISA profile are not available. Use the UART to print.

Switch on Platform devices on the bus in the Memory setting and the single-cycle, multicycle and pipelined views get the same devices and board, polled with lw and sw; traps and interrupts exist only in the profile with traps.
One cycle per instruction and 3 to take a trap; the UART takes 4 cycles per byte. These are the model's own numbers, not measurements of any real core.
The group Devices and traps opens short programs: a running light, switches and a button by polling, a button interrupt, the timer, a system call as a trap, and a serial port.

blocks.p: The NPU tool (the switcher's NPU entry) is a laboratory system: a 4 × 4 weight-stationary systolic array of INT8 processing elements with 32-bit accumulators, a memory-mapped peripheral at 0x5000_0000 beside the GPIO, the timer and the UART. The processor reaches it with lw and sw only. Its views are ISA, Single-cycle (the single-cycle datapath with the NPU on the data bus), NPU (the peripheral at four levels: subsystem, systolic array, processing element, system) and Analysis.

dl: Bit 0 starts, bit 1 clears the accumulators and done; both bits: clear, then start.
Row i of W: W[i][j] in bits 8j+7 to 8j.
x[j] in bits 7 to 0; the higher bits are ignored; a read gives the value sign-extended.
The INT32 accumulator: each start adds y[i] = Σ W[i][j] x[j].

ul: A start keeps the NPU busy for 2N + 1 = 9 cycles: one to copy the weights into the processing elements, eight for the array. Writes to CTRL, WEIGHT and ACT while it is busy are ignored (the NPU view marks them); a program learns that the run has finished only by reading STATUS.
The controller's step counts 0 to 7 during the run and keeps its last value while the NPU is idle, until the next run starts.
The systolic-array level's Register boundaries option draws where each processing element registers its activation and partial sum: a value crosses one dashed line per step.

In the NPU view only the blocks a cycle uses stay lit: the subsystem shows each transfer on its path (a store through the register interface into WEIGHT, ACT or CTRL; a load of STATUS or RESULT back to the processor; the weights into the PEs in LOADW; x[r] into row r, the multiply-adds and the column sums into RESULT in RUN), with a tag at its destination and the same in words below the drawing; the processing element shows its own step. The subsystem and the system both show two accesses of the cycle: the transfer just completed, whose data the registers now hold (solid, marked Completed), and the access of the instruction executing in the cycle (dashed, its tag marked next, its words This cycle). Signal flow, in the panel heading, animates them (off when the system asks for reduced motion).
Other offsets read 0 and ignore writes. The NPU takes whole words: a byte or half-word access is a bus fault (the simulator's choice).
A read of RESULT while the NPU is busy returns the partly accumulated value and gives a warning; the run may stop there (the simulator's choice).

blocks.p: The Analysis view measures the program in the editor on the laboratory profile (RV32IM with the devices, one cycle per instruction, as on the single-cycle processor), on its own data or on the laboratory data sets of 1, 4 and 16 vectors placed at address 0. Its tabs:

dl: Every executed instruction in one class (send the weights, send x and start, poll STATUS, copy the results, markers, loop control and other), counted over the run, between the GPIO markers and per vector, between two starts. The rules are given under the table; they look at what each instruction does, not at the program's name.
The cycles of the three laboratory templates (shift-and-add, with mul, NPU) and of your program, for 1, 4 and 16 vectors, with the speed-ups and the cycles per vector.

Three illustrative machines (editable), three example kernels and a kernel of yours given by operations and bytes; below, a roof for the laboratory system (one 32-bit word per cycle on the bus, 32 operations per cycle for the array) with the point of your run, and what was counted to place it.
Calculators for Amdahl's law over many lanes, the MACs of a fully connected layer or a 3 × 3 convolution, the accumulator width of INT8 products and the scale and zero point of a quantised range.

blocks.p: Practice exercises for the NPU (the group NPU (laboratory profile) of the practice exercises) run on the laboratory profile; their tests check the words your program stores. No solutions are shipped.
What is not modelled:

ul: Wait states: the bus moves one word per cycle with no delay, as in the laboratory.

Interrupts from the NPU, DMA, double buffering, packed activations and results requantised to INT8; an array size other than 4 on the bus (the systolic-array level explores N = 2, 3 and 4 on its own).
Output-stationary or row-stationary dataflows and tensor cores.
The NPU on the multicycle and pipelined processors: the NPU tool times it on the instruction level and the single-cycle processor only.
Hardware: the signals of the waveforms and the VCD file are the simulator's model, not nets of a hardware description, and simulated cycles are not FPGA measurements.
Your work is kept in this browser: after a refresh or a closed tab, the program, its file name, the cursor, breakpoints, watchpoints, loaded data and the step you had reached come back.
File ▸ Copy share link puts the program, the view and its settings into a link. They travel in the part after #, which the browser never sends to a server.
File ▸ Save program and settings… writes a .json file; File ▸ Open reads it back, and also .s and .c files.

Exports: memory images for $readmemh and binary, the listing, traces (JSON lines, CSV), golden dumps for testbenches and VCD waveforms of the processor signals. The drawings export as SVG or PNG from Display.

Exercises: File ▸ Exercise… lists practice exercises written for MAVILERA, each with a starter program; a teacher's exercise file opens with File ▸ Open. Run the tests checks your program and shows expected against actual for each. No solutions are included.
File ▸ Data in and out… loads a CSV or binary file into a data array before a run, and saves a memory range.

blocks.p: Every computation runs in your browser. MAVILERA has no account, sends no telemetry and uploads nothing. After a first visit the hosted version also opens without a network connection, and a single-file version can be downloaded for computers that have none.
